# Wework DSH 扩展 Demo 这是“Wework 插件开发”Skill 携带的可运行 Core DSH 插件示例，覆盖 Wework 当前公开的全部 UI 扩展点。模型可以复制该目录作为实现参考；桌面应用不会自动启用 它。 先把该目录复制到可写的项目目录，再在 Wework 的“插件 → 管理 → Wework 插件”中 输入复制后目录的绝对路径，例如： ```text file:/absolute/path/to/ui-extension-demo ``` 安装完成后重启 Core DSH。左侧会出现 `DSH Demo`，应用切换器、设置页、Composer、 工作区工具栏、底部面板、新建工作区 Tab 菜单和全局 overlay 也会出现对应示例。 示例还注册了一个可从 Composer、工作区工具栏以及 `Command+Shift+D` （Windows/Linux 为 `Ctrl+Shift+D`）触发的统一命令，并演示上下文条件、配置和 持久化状态。 停用或卸载插件并重启后，所有贡献会随同一 DSH 生命周期一起移除。 关键文件： - `package.json` 声明 DSH bundle、client 依赖和浏览器平台。 - `cordis.patch.yml` 把插件加入 DSH Loader 树。 - `index.js` 是 host 入口；纯 UI 插件可以保持为空。 - `client.js` 通过 `ctx.wework` 注册命令、菜单、快捷键、配置与状态，并通过 `ctx.wework.contributions` 注册宿主描述、通过原生 `ctx.slots.register` 注册自定义 UI。 - 左侧 `DSH Demo` 入口通过公开的 `workspaceTab` 路由参数首次创建独立 Tab， 后续点击复用同一个 Tab，不会覆盖用户当前正在使用的 Tab。 生产插件应更换包名、ID、文案和样式，并只注册实际需要的扩展点。 # Wegent > An open-source AI work system spanning your local desktop, cloud agents, and remote machines. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent includes a desktop workbench and a self-hostable web platform. Wegent Desktop works with local projects, files, commands, tests, and code changes. Wegent Web provides browser-based agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Wegent Backend connects these applications to shared project spaces, models, and execution devices. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## Wegent Desktop Wegent Desktop organizes local coding work by project and task. The task view keeps the conversation, tool activity, tests, changed files, and diffs together; the project-space view provides the board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

A project space in Wegent Desktop with its task board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

## Features - **Desktop workbench** — Organize local projects, tasks, sessions, files, tool activity, tests, and diffs. - **Reusable agents** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, tools, and collaboration settings. - **Project spaces** — Share task boards, files, discussions, automation, execution history, and deliveries. - **Multiple execution targets** — Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend for team access, APIs, permissions, scheduling, and knowledge services. ## Why Wegent **The local coding experience built on Codex is the foundation of Wegent Desktop.** It works directly with the code, files, commands, and development environment in your projects. Connect it to Wegent Backend when coding work needs to move beyond one computer or one person. Once connected, the desktop workbench and Web use the same projects, tasks, and execution devices. - **Run tasks on the right device** — Keep using the code, files, commands, and development environment already on a local machine, or run a task for the same project on a remote work machine or server-managed executor. - **Move a project forward as a team** — Project spaces connect task boards, shared files, discussions, execution status, and deliveries instead of leaving conversations and code changes on separate computers. - **Automate repeated project work** — Project spaces can configure automation and execution queues to keep routine work moving. - **Keep services and data under team control** — Self-host Web and Backend for shared access, permissions, model configuration, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote-device management. If work always stays on one computer, Wegent Desktop provides a familiar Codex coding experience. Connect it to Wegent to extend that experience when tasks must move across people, devices, or a self-hosted environment. ## Wegent Web Wegent Web provides the browser interface for remote agents. Agents can use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools while Wegent Backend manages their tasks and execution.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

## How it works Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench. Electron owns desktop windows, system capabilities, and process management. DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is the embedded application and plugin runtime, and the Wework product UI is composed from a set of DSH plugins. Executor manages tasks and sessions, then drives Codex to perform the actual work in local projects. ```mermaid flowchart LR Electron["Electron
Desktop host"] subgraph DSH["DSH Runtime"] direction TB Core["DSH Core
Plugin discovery, dependency injection, and lifecycle"] App["dsh-app-wework
Wework product shell and UI extension points"] UI["dsh-ui-*
Tasks, project spaces, settings, apps, and automation"] ElectronPlugin["dsh-electron-host
Electron capability bridge"] ExecutorPlugin["dsh-executor-runtime
Task execution and event adapter"] TerminalPlugin["dsh-terminal-runtime
Local interactive terminals"] Core --> App Core --> UI Core --> ElectronPlugin Core --> ExecutorPlugin Core --> TerminalPlugin App --> UI end Executor["Executor
Task and session execution"] Codex["Codex
Coding agent"] Workspace["Local project
Files and commands"] Electron -->|"Starts and hosts"| Core Electron -->|"Starts and supervises"| Executor ElectronPlugin <-->|"Restricted desktop capabilities"| Electron UI <-->|"User actions and UI updates"| ExecutorPlugin ExecutorPlugin -->|"Create, follow up, approve, cancel"| Executor Executor -->|"Status, messages, tool events, results"| ExecutorPlugin Executor <-->|"Launch, control, and events"| Codex Codex <-->|"Read, modify, and execute"| Workspace TerminalPlugin <-->|"PTY"| Workspace ``` DSH does not execute coding tasks itself. `dsh-app-wework` defines the product shell and extension points, `dsh-ui-*` provides the product modules, `dsh-electron-host` bridges restricted Electron capabilities, `dsh-executor-runtime` communicates bidirectionally with Executor throughout execution, and `dsh-terminal-runtime` manages local interactive terminals. Executor is the task execution layer, while Codex is the concrete coding agent it drives. Wework can also connect to Wegent Backend for shared project spaces, models, and remote execution devices. Wegent Web is a separate browser interface built on the same Backend. ## Quick start ### Wegent Desktop 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app and add or select a local project. 3. Create a task and describe the work to perform. 4. Review the agent activity, command output, and file changes. ### Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Development Requires Node.js 22.15+ (22.x) or 23.8+ (Node.js 24 recommended), and pnpm: ```bash pnpm install pnpm --filter wework dev ``` To run the macOS desktop app: ```bash pnpm --filter wework dev:mac ``` See [wework/README.md](wework/README.md) for desktop development, build, and release instructions. `wework/` is the current desktop application source directory. ## Repository map ### Products and services | Directory | Responsibility | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `wework/` | Wegent Desktop (Electron, Vite, React) | | `wework-mobile/` | Independent Expo application for iOS and Android | | `frontend/` | Wegent Web (Next.js, React) | | `backend/` | Default public API, business logic, and data models | | `backend-rs/` | Rust hybrid gateway and APIs that have completed migration | | `executor/` | Rust task executor, local-device runtime, and Codex integration | | `executor_manager/` | Server-side executor scheduling, sandboxes, and orchestration | | `chat_shell/` | Lightweight chat and agent runtime | | `knowledge_runtime/` | Knowledge indexing and retrieval API | | `knowledge_doc_converter/` | Document parsing and asynchronous conversion service | ### Shared code and developer tools | Directory | Responsibility | | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `knowledge_engine/` | Reusable Python kernel for parsing, indexing, vector stores, and retrieval | | `shared/` | Python models, protocols, utilities, and telemetry shared by services | | `packages/` | TypeScript chat and collaboration modules shared by Web and Desktop | | `sdk/` | Plugin authentication, build, creation, and DingTalk workspace SDKs | | `wegent-cli/` | Python CLI for managing Wegent CRD resources | ### Infrastructure, tests, and documentation | Directory | Responsibility | | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `docker/` | Service images, standalone resources, and the `docker/telemetry/` observability stack | | `scripts/` | Installation, release, acceptance, repository-policy, and development automation | | `tests/` | Cross-service Playwright integration tests and installation tests | | `docs/` | English and Chinese user docs, developer docs, architecture, and historical designs | | `patches/` | Third-party dependency patches used by pnpm `patchedDependencies` | | `LICENSES/` | Third-party license texts required for repository distribution | | `.github/` | CI, release workflows, composite actions, and repository automation | ### Root entry points | File | Responsibility | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | `start.sh`, `install.sh` | Local startup and self-hosted installation | | `build_image.sh`, `build_image_mac.sh` | Multi-architecture and host Docker image builds | | `docker-compose*.yml` | Default, build, and E2E Compose orchestration | | `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | JavaScript/TypeScript workspace definition | | `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` | Repository-level Python tooling and lock metadata | | `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` | Contributor rules and compatibility [Developer guide](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/README.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/en/wegent/troubleshooting.md) ## Contributing Bug reports, documentation improvements, code contributions, and new # Wegent > An open-source AI work system spanning your local desktop, cloud agents, and remote machines. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent includes a desktop workbench and a self-hostable web platform. Wegent Desktop works with local projects, files, commands, tests, and code changes. Wegent Web provides browser-based agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Wegent Backend connects these applications to shared project spaces, models, and execution devices. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## Wegent Desktop Wegent Desktop organizes local coding work by project and task. The task view keeps the conversation, tool activity, tests, changed files, and diffs together; the project-space view provides the board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

A project space in Wegent Desktop with its task board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

## Features - **Desktop workbench** — Organize local projects, tasks, sessions, files, tool activity, tests, and diffs. - **Reusable agents** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, tools, and collaboration settings. - **Project spaces** — Share task boards, files, discussions, automation, execution history, and deliveries. - **Multiple execution targets** — Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend for team access, APIs, permissions, scheduling, and knowledge services. ## Why Wegent **The local coding experience built on Codex is the foundation of Wegent Desktop.** It works directly with the code, files, commands, and development environment in your projects. Connect it to Wegent Backend when coding work needs to move beyond one computer or one person. Once connected, the desktop workbench and Web use the same projects, tasks, and execution devices. - **Run tasks on the right device** — Keep using the code, files, commands, and development environment already on a local machine, or run a task for the same project on a remote work machine or server-managed executor. - **Move a project forward as a team** — Project spaces connect task boards, shared files, discussions, execution status, and deliveries instead of leaving conversations and code changes on separate computers. - **Automate repeated project work** — Project spaces can configure automation and execution queues to keep routine work moving. - **Keep services and data under team control** — Self-host Web and Backend for shared access, permissions, model configuration, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote-device management. If work always stays on one computer, Wegent Desktop provides a familiar Codex coding experience. Connect it to Wegent to extend that experience when tasks must move across people, devices, or a self-hosted environment. ## Wegent Web Wegent Web provides the browser interface for remote agents. Agents can use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools while Wegent Backend manages their tasks and execution.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

## How it works Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench. Electron owns desktop windows, system capabilities, and process management. DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is the embedded application and plugin runtime, and the Wework product UI is composed from a set of DSH plugins. Executor manages tasks and sessions, then drives Codex to perform the actual work in local projects. ```mermaid flowchart LR Electron["Electron
Desktop host"] subgraph DSH["DSH Runtime"] direction TB Core["DSH Core
Plugin discovery, dependency injection, and lifecycle"] App["dsh-app-wework
Wework product shell and UI extension points"] UI["dsh-ui-*
Tasks, project spaces, settings, apps, and automation"] ElectronPlugin["dsh-electron-host
Electron capability bridge"] ExecutorPlugin["dsh-executor-runtime
Task execution and event adapter"] TerminalPlugin["dsh-terminal-runtime
Local interactive terminals"] Core --> App Core --> UI Core --> ElectronPlugin Core --> ExecutorPlugin Core --> TerminalPlugin App --> UI end Executor["Executor
Task and session execution"] Codex["Codex
Coding agent"] Workspace["Local project
Files and commands"] Electron -->|"Starts and hosts"| Core Electron -->|"Starts and supervises"| Executor ElectronPlugin <-->|"Restricted desktop capabilities"| Electron UI <-->|"User actions and UI updates"| ExecutorPlugin ExecutorPlugin -->|"Create, follow up, approve, cancel"| Executor Executor -->|"Status, messages, tool events, results"| ExecutorPlugin Executor <-->|"Launch, control, and events"| Codex Codex <-->|"Read, modify, and execute"| Workspace TerminalPlugin <-->|"PTY"| Workspace ``` DSH does not execute coding tasks itself. `dsh-app-wework` defines the product shell and extension points, `dsh-ui-*` provides the product modules, `dsh-electron-host` bridges restricted Electron capabilities, `dsh-executor-runtime` communicates bidirectionally with Executor throughout execution, and `dsh-terminal-runtime` manages local interactive terminals. Executor is the task execution layer, while Codex is the concrete coding agent it drives. Wework can also connect to Wegent Backend for shared project spaces, models, and remote execution devices. Wegent Web is a separate browser interface built on the same Backend. ## Quick start ### Wegent Desktop 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app and add or select a local project. 3. Create a task and describe the work to perform. 4. Review the agent activity, command output, and file changes. ### Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Development Requires Node.js 22.15+ (22.x) or 23.8+ (Node.js 24 recommended), and pnpm: ```bash pnpm install pnpm --filter wework dev ``` To run the macOS desktop app: ```bash pnpm --filter wework dev:mac ``` See [wework/README.md](wework/README.md) for desktop development, build, and release instructions. `wework/` is the current desktop application source directory. ## Repository map ### Products and services | Directory | Responsibility | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `wework/` | Wegent Desktop (Electron, Vite, React) | | `wework-mobile/` | Independent Expo application for iOS and Android | | `frontend/` | Wegent Web (Next.js, React) | | `backend/` | Default public API, business logic, and data models | | `backend-rs/` | Rust hybrid gateway and APIs that have completed migration | | `executor/` | Rust task executor, local-device runtime, and Codex integration | | `executor_manager/` | Server-side executor scheduling, sandboxes, and orchestration | | `chat_shell/` | Lightweight chat and agent runtime | | `knowledge_runtime/` | Knowledge indexing and retrieval API | | `knowledge_doc_converter/` | Document parsing and asynchronous conversion service | ### Shared code and developer tools | Directory | Responsibility | | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `knowledge_engine/` | Reusable Python kernel for parsing, indexing, vector stores, and retrieval | | `shared/` | Python models, protocols, utilities, and telemetry shared by services | | `packages/` | TypeScript chat and collaboration modules shared by Web and Desktop | | `sdk/` | Plugin authentication, build, creation, and DingTalk workspace SDKs | | `wegent-cli/` | Python CLI for managing Wegent CRD resources | ### Infrastructure, tests, and documentation | Directory | Responsibility | | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `docker/` | Service images, standalone resources, and the `docker/telemetry/` observability stack | | `scripts/` | Installation, release, acceptance, repository-policy, and development automation | | `tests/` | Cross-service Playwright integration tests and installation tests | | `docs/` | English and Chinese user docs, developer docs, architecture, and historical designs | | `patches/` | Third-party dependency patches used by pnpm `patchedDependencies` | | `LICENSES/` | Third-party license texts required for repository distribution | | `.github/` | CI, release workflows, composite actions, and repository automation | ### Root entry points | File | Responsibility | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | `start.sh`, `install.sh` | Local startup and self-hosted installation | | `build_image.sh`, `build_image_mac.sh` | Multi-architecture and host Docker image builds | | `docker-compose*.yml` | Default, build, and E2E Compose orchestration | | `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | JavaScript/TypeScript workspace definition | | `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` | Repository-level Python tooling and lock metadata | | `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` | Contributor rules and compatibility symlink | ## Documentation - [Wegent Desktop documentation](docs/en/wework/README.md) - [Desktop development and release](wework/README.md) - [Wegent quick start](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/quick-start.md) - [Installation and deployment](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) - [Core concepts](docs/en/wegent/concepts/core-concepts.md) - [Developer guide](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/README.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/en/wegent/troubleshooting.md) ## Contributing Bug reports, documentation improvements, code contributions, and new ways of using Wegent are all welcome. - [Contributing Guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) - [Security Policy](SECURITY.md) - [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) - DingTalk Community: “wework社区交流”, group ID `190890002451` - [Discord Community](https://discord.gg/MVzJzyqEUp) - [License](LICENSE) ## Contributors Thanks to everyone who helps Wegent grow.

# Wegent > An open-source AI work system spanning your local desktop, cloud agents, and remote machines. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent includes a desktop workbench and a self-hostable web platform. Wegent Desktop works with local projects, files, commands, tests, and code changes. Wegent Web provides browser-based agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Wegent Backend connects these applications to shared project spaces, models, and execution devices. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## Wegent Desktop Wegent Desktop organizes local coding work by project and task. The task view keeps the conversation, tool activity, tests, changed files, and diffs together; the project-space view provides the board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

A project space in Wegent Desktop with its task board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

## Features - **Desktop workbench** — Organize local projects, tasks, sessions, files, tool activity, tests, and diffs. - **Reusable agents** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, tools, and collaboration settings. - **Project spaces** — Share task boards, files, discussions, automation, execution history, and deliveries. - **Multiple execution targets** — Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend for team access, APIs, permissions, scheduling, and knowledge services. ## Why Wegent **The local coding experience built on Codex is the foundation of Wegent Desktop.** It works directly with the code, files, commands, and development environment in your projects. Connect it to Wegent Backend when coding work needs to move beyond one computer or one person. Once connected, the desktop workbench and Web use the same projects, tasks, and execution devices. - **Run tasks on the right device** — Keep using the code, files, commands, and development environment already on a local machine, or run a task for the same project on a remote work machine or server-managed executor. - **Move a project forward as a team** — Project spaces connect task boards, shared files, discussions, execution status, and deliveries instead of leaving conversations and code changes on separate computers. - **Automate repeated project work** — Project spaces can configure automation and execution queues to keep routine work moving. - **Keep services and data under team control** — Self-host Web and Backend for shared access, permissions, model configuration, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote-device management. If work always stays on one computer, Wegent Desktop provides a familiar Codex coding experience. Connect it to Wegent to extend that experience when tasks must move across people, devices, or a self-hosted environment. ## Wegent Web Wegent Web provides the browser interface for remote agents. Agents can use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools while Wegent Backend manages their tasks and execution.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

## How it works Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench. Electron owns desktop windows, system capabilities, and process management. DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is the embedded application and plugin runtime, and the Wework product UI is composed from a set of DSH plugins. Executor manages tasks and sessions, then drives Codex to perform the actual work in local projects. ```mermaid flowchart LR Electron["Electron
Desktop host"] subgraph DSH["DSH Runtime"] direction TB Core["DSH Core
Plugin discovery, dependency injection, and lifecycle"] App["dsh-app-wework
Wework product shell and UI extension points"] UI["dsh-ui-*
Tasks, project spaces, settings, apps, and automation"] ElectronPlugin["dsh-electron-host
Electron capability bridge"] ExecutorPlugin["dsh-executor-runtime
Task execution and event adapter"] TerminalPlugin["dsh-terminal-runtime
Local interactive terminals"] Core --> App Core --> UI Core --> ElectronPlugin Core --> ExecutorPlugin Core --> TerminalPlugin App --> UI end Executor["Executor
Task and session execution"] Codex["Codex
Coding agent"] Workspace["Local project
Files and commands"] Electron -->|"Starts and hosts"| Core Electron -->|"Starts and supervises"| Executor ElectronPlugin <-->|"Restricted desktop capabilities"| Electron UI <-->|"User actions and UI updates"| ExecutorPlugin ExecutorPlugin -->|"Create, follow up, approve, cancel"| Executor Executor -->|"Status, messages, tool events, results"| ExecutorPlugin Executor <-->|"Launch, control, and events"| Codex Codex <-->|"Read, modify, and execute"| Workspace TerminalPlugin <-->|"PTY"| Workspace ``` DSH does not execute coding tasks itself. `dsh-app-wework` defines the product shell and extension points, `dsh-ui-*` provides the product modules, `dsh-electron-host` bridges restricted Electron capabilities, `dsh-executor-runtime` communicates bidirectionally with Executor throughout execution, and `dsh-terminal-runtime` manages local interactive terminals. Executor is the task execution layer, while Codex is the concrete coding agent it drives. Wework can also connect to Wegent Backend for shared project spaces, models, and remote execution devices. Wegent Web is a separate browser interface built on the same Backend. ## Quick start ### Wegent Desktop 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app and add or select a local project. 3. Create a task and describe the work to perform. 4. Review the agent activity, command output, and file changes. ### Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Development Requires Node.js 22.15+ (22.x) or 23.8+ (Node.js 24 recommended), and pnpm: ```bash pnpm install pnpm --filter wework dev ``` To run the macOS desktop app: ```bash pnpm --filter wework dev:mac ``` See [wework/README.md](wework/README.md) for desktop development, build, and release instructions. `wework/` is the current desktop application source directory. ## Repository map ### Products and services | Directory | Responsibility | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `wework/` | Wegent Desktop (Electron, Vite, React) | | `wework-mobile/` | Independent Expo application for iOS and Android | | `frontend/` | Wegent Web (Next.js, React) | | `backend/` | Default public API, business logic, and data models | | `backend-rs/` | Rust hybrid gateway and APIs that have completed migration | | `executor/` | Rust task executor, local-device runtime, and Codex integration | | `executor_manager/` | Server-side executor scheduling, sandboxes, and orchestration | | `chat_shell/` | Lightweight chat and agent runtime | | `knowledge_runtime/` | Knowledge indexing and retrieval API | | `knowledge_doc_converter/` | Document parsing and asynchronous conversion service | ### Shared code and developer tools | Directory | Responsibility | | ------------------- | `scripts/` | Installation, release, acceptance, repository-policy, and development automation | | `tests/` | Cross-service Playwright integration tests and installation tests | | `docs/` | English and `build_image_mac.sh` | Multi-architecture and host Docker image builds | | `docker-compose*.yml` | Default, build, and E2E Compose orchestration | | `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | # Wework Core DSH terminal runtime This first-party Core DSH plugin owns Wework's local interactive PTY sessions. The packaged Wework frontend calls its same-origin HTTP/SSE API at `/wework/terminal/v1`. The executor remains responsible for task, Codex, local-device and cloud-device execution. It does not proxy desktop terminal input or output. # Wegent > An open-source AI work system spanning your local desktop, cloud agents, and remote machines. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent includes a desktop workbench and a self-hostable web platform. Wegent Desktop works with local projects, files, commands, tests, and code changes. Wegent Web provides browser-based agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Wegent Backend connects these applications to shared project spaces, models, and execution devices. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## Wegent Desktop Wegent Desktop organizes local coding work by project and task. The task view keeps the conversation, tool activity, tests, changed files, and diffs together; the project-space view provides the board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

A project space in Wegent Desktop with its task board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

## Features - **Desktop workbench** — Organize local projects, tasks, sessions, files, tool activity, tests, and diffs. - **Reusable agents** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, tools, and collaboration settings. - **Project spaces** — Share task boards, files, discussions, automation, execution history, and deliveries. - **Multiple execution targets** — Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend for team access, APIs, permissions, scheduling, and knowledge services. ## Why Wegent **The local coding experience built on Codex is the foundation of Wegent Desktop.** It works directly with the code, files, commands, and development environment in your projects. Connect it to Wegent Backend when coding work needs to move beyond one computer or one person. Once connected, the desktop workbench and Web use the same projects, tasks, and execution devices. - **Run tasks on the right device** — Keep using the code, files, commands, and development environment already on a local machine, or run a task for the same project on a remote work machine or server-managed executor. - **Move a project forward as a team** — Project spaces connect task boards, shared files, discussions, execution status, and deliveries instead of leaving conversations and code changes on separate computers. - **Automate repeated project work** — Project spaces can configure automation and execution queues to keep routine work moving. - **Keep services and data under team control** — Self-host Web and Backend for shared access, permissions, model configuration, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote-device management. If work always stays on one computer, Wegent Desktop provides a familiar Codex coding experience. Connect it to Wegent to extend that experience when tasks must move across people, devices, or a self-hosted environment. ## Wegent Web Wegent Web provides the browser interface for remote agents. Agents can use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools while Wegent Backend manages their tasks and execution.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

## How it works Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench. Electron owns desktop windows, system capabilities, and process management. DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is the embedded application and plugin runtime, and the Wework product UI is composed from a set of DSH plugins. Executor manages tasks and sessions, then drives Codex to perform the actual work in local projects. ```mermaid flowchart LR Electron["Electron
Desktop host"] subgraph DSH["DSH Runtime"] direction TB Core["DSH Core
Plugin discovery, dependency injection, and lifecycle"] App["dsh-app-wework
Wework product shell and UI extension points"] UI["dsh-ui-*
Tasks, project spaces, settings, apps, and automation"] ElectronPlugin["dsh-electron-host
Electron capability bridge"] ExecutorPlugin["dsh-executor-runtime
Task execution and event adapter"] TerminalPlugin["dsh-terminal-runtime
Local interactive terminals"] Core --> App Core --> UI Core --> ElectronPlugin Core --> ExecutorPlugin Core --> TerminalPlugin App --> UI end Executor["Executor
Task and session execution"] Codex["Codex
Coding agent"] Workspace["Local project
Files and commands"] Electron -->|"Starts and hosts"| Core Electron -->|"Starts and supervises"| Executor ElectronPlugin <-->|"Restricted desktop capabilities"| Electron UI <-->|"User actions and UI updates"| ExecutorPlugin ExecutorPlugin -->|"Create, follow up, approve, cancel"| Executor Executor -->|"Status, messages, tool events, results"| ExecutorPlugin Executor <-->|"Launch, control, and events"| Codex Codex <-->|"Read, modify, and execute"| Workspace TerminalPlugin <-->|"PTY"| Workspace ``` DSH does not execute coding tasks itself. `dsh-app-wework` defines the product shell and extension points, `dsh-ui-*` provides the product modules, `dsh-electron-host` bridges restricted Electron capabilities, `dsh-executor-runtime` communicates bidirectionally with Executor throughout execution, and `dsh-terminal-runtime` manages local interactive terminals. Executor is the task execution layer, while Codex is the concrete coding agent it drives. Wework can also connect to Wegent Backend for shared project spaces, models, and remote execution devices. Wegent Web is a separate browser interface built on the same Backend. ## Quick start ### Wegent Desktop 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app and add or select a local project. 3. Create a task and describe the work to perform. 4. Review the agent activity, command output, and file changes. ### Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Development Requires Node.js 22.15+ (22.x) or 23.8+ (Node.js 24 recommended), and pnpm: ```bash pnpm install pnpm --filter wework dev ``` To run the macOS desktop app: ```bash pnpm --filter wework dev:mac ``` See [wework/README.md](wework/README.md) for desktop development, build, and release instructions. `wework/` is the current desktop application source directory. ## Repository map ### Products and scheduling, sandboxes, and orchestration | | `chat_shell/` | Lightweight chat and agent runtime | | `knowledge_runtime/` | Knowledge indexing and retrieval API | | `knowledge_doc_converter/` | # Wegent > An open-source AI work system spanning your local desktop, cloud agents, and remote machines. English | [简体中文](README_zh.md) [![CI](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/wecode-ai/Wegent)](LICENSE) [![GitHub Issues](https://img.shields.io/github/issues/wecode-ai/Wegent)](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) Wegent includes a desktop workbench and a self-hostable web platform. Wegent Desktop works with local projects, files, commands, tests, and code changes. Wegent Web provides browser-based agents, knowledge, automation, and administration. Wegent Backend connects these applications to shared project spaces, models, and execution devices. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) · [Documentation](https://wecode-ai.github.io/wegent-docs/) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## Wegent Desktop Wegent Desktop organizes local coding work by project and task. The task view keeps the conversation, tool activity, tests, changed files, and diffs together; the project-space view provides the board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

Running and reviewing a local coding task in Wegent Desktop.

A project space in Wegent Desktop with its task board, shared files, automation, and execution status.

## Features - **Desktop workbench** — Organize local projects, tasks, sessions, files, tool activity, tests, and diffs. - **Reusable agents** — Combine models, prompts, Skills, knowledge, tools, and collaboration settings. - **Project spaces** — Share task boards, files, discussions, automation, execution history, and deliveries. - **Multiple execution targets** — Run tasks locally, on remote work machines, or with server-managed executors. - **Self-hosting** — Deploy Wegent Web and Backend for team access, APIs, permissions, scheduling, and knowledge services. ## Why Wegent **The local coding experience built on Codex is the foundation of Wegent Desktop.** It works directly with the code, files, commands, and development environment in your projects. Connect it to Wegent Backend when coding work needs to move beyond one computer or one person. Once connected, the desktop workbench and Web use the same projects, tasks, and execution devices. - **Run tasks on the right device** — Keep using the code, files, commands, and development environment already on a local machine, or run a task for the same project on a remote work machine or server-managed executor. - **Move a project forward as a team** — Project spaces connect task boards, shared files, discussions, execution status, and deliveries instead of leaving conversations and code changes on separate computers. - **Automate repeated project work** — Project spaces can configure automation and execution queues to keep routine work moving. - **Keep services and data under team control** — Self-host Web and Backend for shared access, permissions, model configuration, scheduling, knowledge services, and remote-device management. If work always stays on one computer, Wegent Desktop provides a familiar Codex coding experience. Connect it to Wegent to extend that experience when tasks must move across people, devices, or a self-hosted environment. ## Wegent Web Wegent Web provides the browser interface for remote agents. Agents can use configured models, knowledge, Skills, and tools while Wegent Backend manages their tasks and execution.

A Wegent remote agent uses tools to generate a Gantt chart.

## How it works Wework is the Wegent desktop workbench. Electron owns desktop windows, system capabilities, and process management. DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is the embedded application and plugin runtime, and the Wework product UI is composed from a set of DSH plugins. Executor manages tasks and sessions, then drives Codex to perform the actual work in local projects. ```mermaid flowchart LR Electron["Electron
Desktop host"] subgraph DSH["DSH Runtime"] direction TB Core["DSH Core
Plugin discovery, dependency injection, and lifecycle"] App["dsh-app-wework
Wework product shell and UI extension points"] UI["dsh-ui-*
Tasks, project spaces, settings, apps, and automation"] ElectronPlugin["dsh-electron-host
Electron capability bridge"] ExecutorPlugin["dsh-executor-runtime
Task execution and event adapter"] TerminalPlugin["dsh-terminal-runtime
Local interactive terminals"] Core --> App Core --> UI Core --> ElectronPlugin Core --> ExecutorPlugin Core --> TerminalPlugin App --> UI end Executor["Executor
Task and session execution"] Codex["Codex
Coding agent"] Workspace["Local project
Files and commands"] Electron -->|"Starts and hosts"| Core Electron -->|"Starts and supervises"| Executor ElectronPlugin <-->|"Restricted desktop capabilities"| Electron UI <-->|"User actions and UI updates"| ExecutorPlugin ExecutorPlugin -->|"Create, follow up, approve, cancel"| Executor Executor -->|"Status, messages, tool events, results"| ExecutorPlugin Executor <-->|"Launch, control, and events"| Codex Codex <-->|"Read, modify, and execute"| Workspace TerminalPlugin <-->|"PTY"| Workspace ``` DSH does not execute coding tasks itself. `dsh-app-wework` defines the product shell and extension points, `dsh-ui-*` provides the product modules, `dsh-electron-host` bridges restricted Electron capabilities, `dsh-executor-runtime` communicates bidirectionally with Executor throughout execution, and `dsh-terminal-runtime` manages local interactive terminals. Executor is the task execution layer, while Codex is the concrete coding agent it drives. Wework can also connect to Wegent Backend for shared project spaces, models, and remote execution devices. Wegent Web is a separate browser interface built on the same Backend. ## Quick start ### Wegent Desktop 1. [Download the latest Wegent Desktop installer](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/releases/latest) and install it. 2. Open the app and add or select a local project. 3. Create a task and describe the work to perform. 4. Review the agent activity, command output, and file changes. ### Wegent Web and Backend To start the self-hosted web application and Backend in standalone mode with Docker: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --standalone ``` Open http://localhost:3000 and follow the setup flow to create the administrator password and configure a model. See the [Installation Guide](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) and [Standalone Mode](docs/en/wegent/deployment/standalone-mode.md) for other deployment options. ## Development Requires Node.js 22.15+ (22.x) or 23.8+ (Node.js 24 recommended), and pnpm: ```bash pnpm install pnpm --filter wework dev ``` To run the macOS desktop app: ```bash pnpm --filter wework dev:mac ``` See [wework/README.md](wework/README.md) for desktop development, build, and release instructions. `wework/` is the current desktop application source directory. ## Repository map ### Products and services | Directory | Responsibility | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `wework/` | Wegent Desktop (Electron, Vite, React) | | `wework-mobile/` | Independent Expo application for iOS and Android | | `frontend/` | Wegent Web (Next.js, React) | | `backend/` | Default public API, business logic, and data models | | `backend-rs/` | Rust hybrid gateway and APIs that have completed migration | | `executor/` | Rust task executor, local-device runtime, and Codex integration | | `executor_manager/` | Server-side executor scheduling, sandboxes, and orchestration | | `chat_shell/` | Lightweight chat and agent runtime | | `knowledge_runtime/` | Knowledge indexing and retrieval API | | `knowledge_doc_converter/` | Document parsing and asynchronous conversion service | ### Shared code and developer tools | Directory | Responsibility | | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `knowledge_engine/` | Reusable Python kernel for parsing, indexing, vector stores, and retrieval | | `shared/` | Python models, protocols, utilities, and telemetry shared by services | | `packages/` | TypeScript chat and collaboration modules shared by Web and Desktop | | `sdk/` | Plugin authentication, build, creation, and DingTalk workspace SDKs | | `wegent-cli/` | Python CLI for managing Wegent CRD resources | ### Infrastructure, tests, and documentation | Directory | Responsibility | | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `docker/` | Service images, standalone resources, and the `docker/telemetry/` observability stack | | `scripts/` | Installation, release, acceptance, repository-policy, and development automation | | `tests/` | Cross-service Playwright integration tests and installation tests | | `docs/` | English and Chinese user docs, developer docs, architecture, and historical designs | | `patches/` | Third-party dependency patches used by pnpm `patchedDependencies` | | `LICENSES/` | Third-party license texts required for repository distribution | | `.github/` | CI, release workflows, composite actions, and repository automation | ### Root entry points | File | Responsibility | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | `start.sh`, `install.sh` | Local startup and self-hosted installation | | `build_image.sh`, `build_image_mac.sh` | Multi-architecture and host Docker image builds | | `docker-compose*.yml` | Default, build, and E2E Compose orchestration | | `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | JavaScript/TypeScript workspace definition | | `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` | Repository-level Python tooling and lock metadata | | `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` | Contributor rules and compatibility symlink | ## Documentation - [Wegent Desktop documentation](docs/en/wework/README.md) - [Desktop development and release](wework/README.md) - [Wegent quick start](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/quick-start.md) - [Installation and deployment](docs/en/wegent/getting-started/installation.md) - [Core concepts](docs/en/wegent/concepts/core-concepts.md) - [Developer guide](docs/en/wegent/developer-guide/README.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/en/wegent/troubleshooting.md) ## Contributing Bug reports, documentation improvements, code contributions, and new ways of using Wegent are all welcome. - [Contributing Guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) - [Security Policy](SECURITY.md) - [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/wecode-ai/Wegent/issues) - DingTalk Community: # dsh-resume

The manifest in this folder is the one the compatibility sample audits. Its
`engines.dsh` range is the real one from `L3n3L/dsh-resume@0.1.3`:

```json
"engines": {
  "dsh": ">=0.1.0-rc.6 <0.2.0-0"
}
```

# dsh-plugin-toolkit

[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-plugin-toolkit)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-plugin-toolkit)
[![downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dw/dsh-plugin-toolkit)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-plugin-toolkit)
[![CI](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/dsh-plugin-toolkit)](LICENSE)


![dsh-plugin-toolkit](docs/card.png)

English · [中文](./README.zh.md)

Everything a [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) plugin needs between `init` and a version the market index accepts: scaffolding, a test harness for the client bundle, a way to see a change without restarting the app, and a release that does not depend on remembering fourteen steps.

```sh
npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest init ./my-panel --name my-panel   # a plugin that already passes the checks
npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest verify .                          # pack it, install the tarball, mount the panel
npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest release --pr --merge              # tag, wait for npm, update the index, open and merge the PR
```

## The panel

![The Plugin doctor tab, on a plugin that fails two checks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit/main/docs/panel.png)

The same checks, in the right sidebar: type a folder, an `owner/repo`, or a GitHub link, and it says which one would fail and why. Nothing is installed and nothing is written.

## Three paths

| You are… | Start with | Then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| writing your first plugin | [`init`](#1-write-a-plugin) | `doctor`, `fix`, `verify` |
| changing a panel that is already installed | [`dev`](#2-develop-a-panel) | `mount`, the testkit, `audit` |
| shipping a version | [`verify`](#3-ship-a-version) | `release`, `index` |

It also installs as a plugin. `dsh plugin add dsh-plugin-toolkit` puts a
**插件体检 / Plugin doctor** panel under the conversation and a tab in the right
sidebar. Give it a folder that holds a plugin's `package.json`, or just
`owner/repo` — or a repository name, which it searches GitHub for and lists the
candidates to pick from. It then runs the same checks `verify` runs and says
which one would break the install, with the reason on the line — the same
answers as the CLI, without leaving the app.

```
$ dsh plugin add dsh-plugin-toolkit
```

### 1. Write a plugin

[`init`](#start-from-a-plugin-that-already-passes) writes the files whose absence shows up as a failed first publish — `engines.dsh`, the patch file, a `files` list that ships the code, a client bundle, a test for it, and the CI that runs both. `doctor` then checks the same things without writing anything, and [`verify`](#prove-the-tarball-works-not-just-the-repository) checks the tarball instead of the working copy.

If a plugin already exists, `doctor --fix` turns the failing checks into a
repair plan. It names the file and the edit for every problem, writes nothing
until you add `--write`, and then runs the checks again. `fix --engines` is
still there when the host range is the only thing you need to change.

```sh
npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest init ./my-panel --name my-panel
cd my-panel && npm install && npm test && npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest doctor .
```

### 2. Develop a panel

A plugin's client code is one file that calls `window.__ModuleLoader__.load({factory})` — there is no module to import, so the usual React test setup does not apply. [`testkit`](#test-a-panel-without-a-browser) supplies the missing half, and [`dev`](#edit-a-plugin-that-is-already-installed) pushes a rebuilt bundle into the running app.

```sh
npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest mount ./client.js     # what a user would see, without the app
npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest dev . --host http://127.0.0.1:54133
```

### 3. Ship a version

`verify` first (it is the only check that reads the tarball), then `release`, which tags, waits for the registry, writes the index entry with the publish time the registry reports, and — with `--pr --merge` — opens and merges the pull request.

```sh
npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest verify .
npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest release . --pr --merge
```

## What `verify` actually does

![Five steps, and the failure each one catches](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit/main/docs/pipeline.svg)

The order matters. Packing first means the check reads the file list npm will publish, not the folder you have. Installing the tarball means the root export is imported the way the loader imports it. Mounting means the client bundle is actually executed, in jsdom, with a host that records what it registered.

Each step exists because a plugin once got past the step before it and still installed into nothing.

## Why this exists

Releasing one plugin fifteen times taught me three things the ecosystem's tooling does not cover:

1. **A version is not shipped when npm accepts it.** Registry propagation took two to eight minutes every time. `npm view` answered from a stale local cache, so I repeatedly believed a release had failed when it had not — and once believed it had succeeded when the market still could not see it.
2. **The market index is a second release, done by hand.** Each version needs an entry carrying `publishTimestamp` from the registry and `engines.dsh` from the manifest. Forget the range and the index validator rejects the PR with `Engines mismatch` — after the tag is already public.
3. **Reading a manifest is not the same as checking it.** A plugin can have a valid `package.json` and still be uninstallable: `files` that omit the entry the manifest points at, a bundle patch that does not exist, a README that never states the host range it declares.

The five failures behind these checks — a red dot with no panel, a row the host drops, an app that disables every plugin after one unguarded `apply()`, a tab nothing can open, and a checker that was wrong — are written up with their exact error text and how to reproduce each one: [Five plugins that installed and did nothing](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit/blob/main/docs/why-it-exists.md).

### Four ways a plugin installs and still does nothing

Each of these shipped in a real version of this toolkit before the check below existed. A manifest check passes on all four.

| What you see | What it was | Caught by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The tab is a red dot and the panel never opens | `exports["."]` pointed at the CLI, so the loader's row had no plugin to apply | `root export` |
| The plugin is installed, the app never serves it | `dsh.client` declared, `exports["./client"]` missing — the host drops the row | `client declaration` |
| The app says the third-party plugin is unsupported and disables all of them | `apply()` read `ctx.webServer` without declaring it; cordis throws instead of returning `undefined` | `verify` (calls `apply` on a context that has no services) |
| The tab registers, and nothing in the UI opens it | `sidebarRightTabs.register()` registers a *type*; the sidebar lists what `tabs.guide()` returns | a testkit test, not `doctor` |

The first three are static: `doctor` and `verify` catch them without the app running. The fourth is a UI contract, so it needs the panel mounted and the registration inspected — that is what [`testkit`](#test-a-panel-without-a-browser) is for.

## Requirements

- Node.js 18 or newer (the registry is read with `fetch`; no runtime dependencies)
- Git and `gh` on `PATH` for the steps that touch GitHub
- DeepSeek Harness `>=0.2.0` — the version whose market index carries `engines.dsh`, which is what makes the range check meaningful
- For `testkit`: `jsdom`, `react` and `react-dom` as dev dependencies (`npm install --save-dev jsdom react react-dom`)

## Start from a plugin that already passes

```sh
$ npx dsh-plugin-toolkit@latest init ./my-panel --name my-panel --title "My panel"
created 8 file(s) in /Users/you/my-panel
  .github/workflows/ci.yml
  .gitignore
  README.md
  client.js
  cordis.patch.yml
  index.js
  package.json
  test/panel.test.mjs

next: npm install && npm test && npm run doctor
```

What you get is not a snippet: it is a plugin whose `doctor` already passes (`engines.dsh`, the patch file, the `files` list), with a client bundle that registers a sidebar tab, a testkit test for it, and a CI workflow that runs both. `init` refuses a directory that is not empty unless you pass `--force`, and refuses a name npm would refuse — those are the two mistakes that cost the most time later.

## Where it lives

The checker is docked **under the conversation**, above the input bar: a single
row, collapsed by default. Open it and it carries the whole guide — who it is
for, how to use it, what each check means, and what it cannot tell you — plus
the folder field and the results. The same panel is also a **Plugin doctor** tab
in the right sidebar, for when the conversation is busy.

The panel speaks both languages and opens in Chinese; the 中文 / EN switch sits
in the dock's header row (and in the sidebar tab) and the choice is remembered.

Look at it without the app:

```sh
node scripts/preview.mjs /tmp/panel.html   # collapsed, open, with a result, and the tab
```

## Test a panel without a browser

A plugin's client code is one file that calls `window.__ModuleLoader__.load({factory})` — there is no module to import, so the usual React test setup does not apply. `testkit` supplies the missing half: a DOM, the real React, and a host context that records what the panel registers.

```sh
npm install --save-dev jsdom react react-dom
```

```js
import { mountClient, createFetch } from 'dsh-plugin-toolkit/testkit';

const panel = await mountClient({
  file: 'client.js',
  copy: { 'my-plugin': { title: 'My panel' } },
  fetch: createFetch({
    '/my-plugin/report': { body: { score: 71, noise: 3 } },
    '/my-plugin/apply': () => ({ status: 201, body: { score: 92 } }),
  }),
});

await panel.click('[data-testid="optimize"]');
console.assert(panel.text().includes('92'), 'the score on screen did not move');
console.assert(panel.must('[role="status"]').textContent.includes('92'));
await panel.unmount();
```

`unmount()` is async: it lets React finish the work its own unmount schedules before the DOM goes away. Skipping the `await` surfaces as `ReferenceError: window is not defined` *after* the test has already passed, which is a confusing way to learn it.

What you get back: `text()`, `html()`, `query(selector)`, `must(selector)` (throws with the rendered HTML when it misses), `click(selector)`, `type(selector, value)`, `press(selector, key)`, `focus`, `attributes(selector)`, `snapshot(dir, name)` for a normalised DOM baseline, and `host` for assertions about what the bundle registered.

### Keep a visual baseline

The DOM is the baseline: normalising class order and whitespace gives a file that fails for the reasons a screenshot would — a lost label, a control that stopped rendering — and can be reviewed in a diff instead of by eye.

```js
import { expectSnapshot } from 'dsh-plugin-toolkit/testkit';

const panel = await mountClient({ file: 'client.js' });
expectSnapshot(panel.html(), '__snapshots__', 'panel');   // throws with the element that moved
await panel.unmount();
```

First run writes nothing: it tells you to re-run with `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1`, so a baseline is always a decision, never a side effect.

### Check what assistive tech sees

```js
panel.expectAria('[role="tab"][aria-selected="true"]', { label: 'Protection', selected: 'true' });
assert.match(panel.must('[role="status"]').textContent, /Score moved 71 → 77/);
```

`expectAria()` compares the attributes a screen reader actually reads — `role`,
`label`, `live`, `selected`, `expanded`, `checked`, `pressed`, `disabled` — and
names the one that differs:

```
[aria-live="polite"]: expected aria text to be "9", but it is "0"
```

A missing attribute is reported as `nothing`, not as an empty string, because
those are different bugs. `panel.aria(selector)` returns the same object when you
want to assert on it yourself.

`must()` throws with the rendered markup when the selector misses, which is the difference between "the assertion failed" and "here is what the user actually got".

Every example below is a file in this repository, run by CI, and the output shown is the output it prints:

| Example | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| `node examples/mount-a-bundle.mjs` | mount a real bundle, read the text, click, read it again |
| `node examples/route-stubs.mjs` | answer the routes a panel asks for, and assert on the requests |
| `node examples/baseline.mjs` | a DOM baseline compared on every run |
| `node examples/aria.mjs` | what assistive tech sees |

```sh
$ node examples/mount-a-bundle.mjs
Demo panel Count 0 0
Demo panel Count 1 1
```

```sh
$ node examples/route-stubs.mjs
Score 71
asked for: 1 route(s), undeclared route answers 404
```

To look at a bundle by hand:

```sh
npx dsh-plugin mount ./client.js            # print the text a user would see
npx dsh-plugin mount ./client.js --html     # print the markup
```

That is how the AIignore panel was checked before release: the real bundle, mounted in Node, against a stubbed `/aiignore/*`:

```
$ npx dsh-plugin mount ../ai-context-doctor/plugin/client.js
AIignore No workspace yet Could not read the report …
```

## Put the badge on a plugin that passes

If `verify` passes on your plugin, this badge says so and links back here:

```md
[![checked with dsh-plugin-toolkit](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit/main/docs/badge.svg)](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit)
```

It is a claim, not a decoration: add it only when `dsh-plugin verify .` exits 0.

## Start from the example

[`dsh-plugin-example`](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-example) is a ~70-line plugin: one sidebar tab, two languages, one behaviour test, CI that runs `verify` through the composite action. It is the shape this toolkit expects, so it is also the fastest way to see whether the toolkit fits your plugin. It is a GitHub template too: **Use this template** starts you on a plugin whose first publish already passes.

```sh
dsh plugin add dsh-plugin-example
```

## See what is installed, and what the app loaded

`doctor` checks one folder you name. The question that actually gets asked is
"why is my plugin not in the sidebar?", and the answer needs three things at once:
what is installed, whether each installed copy is valid, and which of them the
running app actually loaded.

```sh
$ dsh-plugin audit --host http://127.0.0.1:54133
dsh-aiignore           0.37.1    loaded       ok
demo-panel             0.3.0     not loaded   ok  — dsh.profile.bundles in /Users/me/.dsh/profiles/desktop/package.json does not list it, and the loader mounts only listed bundles
                                            fix: add "demo-panel" to dsh.profile.bundles in /Users/me/.dsh/profiles/desktop/package.json (or run `dsh plugin add demo-panel`), then restart the app

1 installed plugin(s) are not in the running app:
```

"Not loaded" has three different causes, and `audit` names the one that applies
instead of offering a blanket restart:

- **Not in `dsh.profile.bundles`.** `pnpm add` (or `npm install`) installs the
  package but does not tell the loader to mount it. Add the package name to
  `dsh.profile.bundles` in `~/.dsh/profiles/<profile>/package.json`, or run
  `dsh plugin add <name>`, then restart the app.
- **No `dsh.bundle`.** The package declares `dsh` but no patch file to mount.
  Add `dsh.bundle.patch` to its `package.json` and ship the patch file, then
  reinstall.
- **Listed, but the app predates the install.** The profile is already correct;
  restart the app once to read the new list.

Advisories (`engines.dsh`, README Requirements) are counted apart from problems:
the market index needs them, the loader does not, so they should not bury a plugin
that is actually broken.

`audit` exits `1` when an installed plugin has a hard failure **or** when the
running app did not load at least one installed plugin, so CI can gate on a
profile where the app silently skipped a plugin. It exits `0` when every
installed plugin is loaded and valid. If no graph was read (`--host` omitted),
the loaded column is `?` and only hard failures change the exit code.

Without `--host` the loaded column is `?`, because guessing would be worse than
saying nothing. Only packages that declare a `dsh` field are audited — the rest of
`node_modules` is ordinary dependencies, and auditing those is noise.

## Edit a plugin that is already installed

The host already swaps a rebuilt bundle without a page reload: it watches each plugin's entry artifact and reports a `rebuilt` frame on `/plugins/events`. `dev` puts the new file where the host is looking, then **proves** the frame arrived instead of asking you to check by eye.

```sh
npx dsh-plugin dev . --host http://127.0.0.1:54133
```

![dsh-plugin dev printing the revision the app reported](docs/dev.gif)

*Recorded from a real run against the running app: the last line is the revision the app sent back on `/plugins/events`, not a message the tool printed on faith.*

```
demo-aiignore: /work/plugin/client.js -> ~/.dsh/profiles/desktop/node_modules/dsh-aiignore/client.js
initial: copied 163647 bytes at 1:18:43 AM
reloaded dsh-aiignore (rev e0c0230c4fc9)
watching /work/plugin
```

That last line is the whole point: the revision came back from the app's own event stream, so "it reloaded" is a fact, not a hope.

A plugin the running app never loaded cannot be reloaded, and the app says so by leaving it out of the graph it sends first. `dev` reads that graph, so a freshly installed plugin gets the sentence that fixes it instead of a timeout:

```
copied, but not confirmed: the running app has not loaded demo-panel, so it will not report a reload; restart the app once after installing it
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--dest <dir>` | write into this installed copy instead of searching `~/.dsh/profiles/*/node_modules/<name>` |
| `--entry <file>` | copy this file instead of `dsh.client.entry`, `client.js`, `lib/client.js` |
| `--build <command>` | run this before each copy (a failed build copies nothing) |
| `--host <url>` | confirm the reload against the app at this URL; without it the copy still happens and the tool says it is unconfirmed |
| `--once` | copy once and exit, for scripts |

Two things it does not do, because the host does not: React state inside the reloaded plugin is lost, and a failed swap does not roll back to the previous bundle.

## Use it in CI

The same checks run as a GitHub Action, so a tag cannot go out on a plugin that would not install:

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit@v1
  with:
    dir: plugin        # the folder holding the plugin's package.json
    command: verify    # pack it, install the tarball, mount the panel
```

`verify` is the default because it is the only check that reads what a user
actually installs: `doctor` reads the working copy, so a `files` list that
forgets `client.js` passes it and fails only after `npm i`.

`command: doctor` stops at the manifest checks (fast, no install), and
`command: index` audits `market/index.json` instead, failing on any version whose
`engines.dsh` is missing or is not a semver range. Pin `version:` if you would
rather not track the latest release.

## Check a plugin you have not cloned

The panel takes three kinds of input: a folder, `owner/repo`, or a GitHub URL.
A bare name is a search, not a guess — it asks GitHub, lists the matches with
their stars, and checks the one you pick. A repository is downloaded once as a
tarball into a temp folder, so nothing is cloned into your workspace and
nothing is installed.

The CLI reads a repository straight from the GitHub API:

```bash
dsh-plugin doctor --remote V1ki/dsh-plugin-subscriptions
```

```text
dsh-plugin doctor: 1 problem(s) in V1ki/dsh-plugin-subscriptions
  ⨯ engines.dsh: engines.dsh is missing, so a host that enforces the range rejects the install as "incompatible with dsh"; declare the range you support, e.g. "engines": { "dsh": ">=0.2.0" }
```

That is the whole reason this mode exists: the plugin hub files failed installs
back into plugin repositories, and the report is a sentence — `plugin install
failed`, `plugin does not support the DSH version in use` — that never names a
file. Reading `package.json` over the API is enough to name it.

What it can see, and what it cannot:

- Manifest checks (`engines.dsh`, `files`, `dsh.client`, `exports`) run on the
  real `package.json`.
- File checks (does `exports["./client"]` point at a file that exists, does the
  root export `apply`) need the tree. A package that runs `prepack`,
  `prepublishOnly`, `prepare` or `build` publishes files it does not commit, so
  those checks are **skipped with a note** instead of calling a working plugin
  broken.
- Public repositories work anonymously, but GitHub allows 60 requests an hour.
  Export `GH_TOKEN` (or `GITHUB_TOKEN`) to audit more than one or two.

To check a whole list in one pass, put one `owner/repo` per line in a file and
pass it with `--from` (`-` reads standard input):

```sh
$ dsh-plugin audit --remote --from repos.txt
```

Repositories are read four at a time by default. `--jobs N` changes that width;
values above `8` are capped at `8`, and `--jobs 1` walks the list one repository
at a time, the timing the command had before batching. The output — and the
`--json` array — still follows the input list, and every verdict is the one the
sequential run produced, so a diff between two runs compares repositories rather
than scheduling.

When GitHub answers `403` or `429`, the shared quota is gone, so the batch stops
starting new repositories and marks every entry it could not read as
`rate-limited` instead of `clean` or `unreadable`. If the response carries
`x-ratelimit-reset` (or `retry-after`), the reset time is printed with the
verdict, and the remaining entries are reported without another request.

### Will this plugin install on my DSH?

The seven compatibility reports all end with the same question. Add `--host
<version>` to a remote audit and it answers that question for one repository.
This is a real run against `L3n3L/dsh-resume`, a plugin whose declared range
stops before DSH 0.2.0, checked against the `0.2.2-alpha.3` canary from the
reports:

```sh
$ dsh-plugin audit --remote L3n3L/dsh-resume --host 0.2.2-alpha.3
incompatible  L3n3L/dsh-resume  0.1.3 (host >=0.1.0-rc.6 <0.2.0-0) [incompatible with dsh 0.2.2-alpha.3; declares ">=0.1.0-rc.6 <0.2.0-0"]

summary: 1 repository — 0 clean, 1 failing (1 problem), 0 unreadable, 0 rate-limited
```

The verdict comes first: `incompatible` means the range in `package.json` does
not accept the host, so the installer rejects the plugin before it unpacks it.
This run exits `1`. The same answer is reproducible without a GitHub request —
the manifest is checked in under `examples/compatibility-sample/`, and this
command feeds it through the real CLI path:

```sh
$ node scripts/compatibility-sample.mjs
```

(`npm run compatibility` runs the same script.) The test suite runs that
command and compares its output with the block above, so the sample cannot
drift from the formatter or from the README.

The line carries the range `package.json` declares and one of `compatible`,
`incompatible`, or `unknown` against that host version. `unknown` is the honest
answer for a missing or malformed range — there is nothing to compare — while a
range that excludes the host is `incompatible`, counted as failing, and exits
`1`. The same flag works in the batch mode, so one `--from` run answers the
whole list:

```sh
$ dsh-plugin audit --remote --from repos.txt --host 0.2.2-alpha.3
```

The compatibility flags are `--remote <owner/repo>` for one repository,
`--from <file>` for a list (`-` reads standard input), `--host <version>` for
the DSH version to compare against, and `--json` for the machine-readable
finding. `--jobs <n>` sets the batch width, and `--patch-dir <dir>` writes the
host-targeted repair for each repository that needs one. The help text lists
the same flags; a test fails if this section names a flag the CLI does not have.

`--host` still names the running app URL for a local `audit`; on `--remote` it
is the DSH version to compare against. With `--json`, each finding gains
`host` and `compatibility` beside `hostRange`.

Each repository gets one line with its verdict — `clean`, `failing`,
`unreadable`, or `rate-limited` — and the run ends with a counted summary:

```text
clean         demo/plugin  1.2.3 (host >=0.2.0)
failing       demo/broken  — engines.dsh: engines.dsh is missing, so a host that enforces the range rejects the install as "incompatible with dsh"
rate-limited  demo/blocked — GitHub rate-limited this request (403) for package.json; set GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN to raise the limit; the limit resets at 2026-11-04T20:00:00.000Z
rate-limited  demo/next    — GitHub rate-limited the batch before this repository was read, so it was not requested; the limit resets at 2026-11-04T20:00:00.000Z

summary: 4 repositories — 1 clean, 1 failing (1 problem), 0 unreadable, 2 rate-limited
```

The parenthesised count is the number of failed checks, not the number of failing
repositories: one repository that fails both `engines.dsh` and its client
declaration prints `1 failing (2 problems)`.

The command exits `1` when any repository is failing, unreadable, or
rate-limited, and `0` only when every repository in the list is clean. `--from`
also accepts the JSON evidence shape (an array, or an object with `rows`) that
the old shell loop printed, so an existing audit file can be replayed without
rewriting it.

### Measured throughput

The measurement uses the first eight repositories from the 3 November
install-failure list — `610la/dsh-notification-center`,
`Anionex/dsh-vision-toolkit`, `ChongCyrus/Vibe-Mathematics`,
`CrazyShout/dsh-ssh-remote`, `Ebony-Vinyl/dsh-our-free-model`,
`FSMargoo/dsh-at-file`, `FylarOpen/dsh-fylar-office-editor` and
`GraySilver/dsh-evolve-modes` — served from memory with a fixed 500 ms delay on
every API request. That makes the number reproducible on any host: it measures
the batch's scheduling, not GitHub's mood. Reproduce it with:

```sh
$ npm run benchmark
```

(`node scripts/benchmark-audit.mjs` runs the same harness without npm's banner.)
The tarball ships both that script and the list it reads, so the command runs in
a checkout and in an installed copy. The test suite packs the package, installs
the tarball into a temp directory and runs the documented command there;
[`docs/benchmark-tarball.md`](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit/blob/main/docs/benchmark-tarball.md)
records the packaging gap this closes.

It runs the same list twice: `--jobs 1`, which is the loop the command used
before batching, and the default `--jobs 4`. Measured on this host:

| run | wall clock | seconds per repository |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before (`--jobs 1`) | 8.03 s | 1.003 s |
| after (default `--jobs 4`) | 2.01 s | 0.251 s |

The after run keeps four reads in flight, so eight repositories finish in two
waves and the per-repository cost falls from about 1.00 s to about 0.25 s. The
test suite reads this table and fails if the after number no longer matches the
default `--jobs` value, so changing the default cannot leave the claim behind.

For a CI job or a repair sweep, add `--json`:

```sh
$ dsh-plugin audit --remote --from repos.txt --json
```
[
  {
    "target": "V1ki/dsh-plugin-subscriptions",
    "version": "0.3.0",
    "hostRange": ">=0.2.0",
    "failures": [],
    "notes": []
  },
  {
    "target": "demo/plugin",
    "version": "1.2.3",
    "hostRange": null,
    "failures": [
      {
        "check": "engines.dsh",
        "message": "engines.dsh is missing, so a host that enforces the range rejects the install as \"incompatible with dsh\"; declare the range you support, e.g. \"engines\": { \"dsh\": \">=0.2.0\" }"
      }
    ],
    "notes": []
  }
]
```

Every repository produces one object with `target`, `version`, `hostRange`,
`failures` (`{ check, message }`) and `notes`, and the command exits `1` when any
repository has a problem. With `--host <version>` each object also carries
`host` and `compatibility`. A rate-limited repository adds `rateLimited: true`
and a `rateLimit` object with the HTTP `status` and, when GitHub sent one,
`resetAt`; it is not marked `unreadable`. A network error is printed in `notes`
and still exits `1`: a repository the tool could not read is never reported as
clean. Packages that build before they pack
keep their file-level checks in `notes` as before.

When the list is a repair queue rather than a report, add `--patch-dir`:

```sh
$ dsh-plugin audit --remote --from repos.txt --patch-dir repairs/
```

It creates the directory and writes one `owner__repo.patch` for every
repository whose `engines.dsh` check fails, with the same diff `fix --remote
--patch` produces. Repositories that are clean, unreadable, or need a repair
the tool cannot make automatically are skipped. The repository itself is still
only read, and `--force` replaces a patch that is already there.

### The 3 November list

The install-failure audit that started this tool covers 67 repositories. Its
list is checked in as
[`docs/ecosystem-audit-2026-11-03.txt`](https://github.com/WJDdidi-1/dsh-plugin-toolkit/blob/main/docs/ecosystem-audit-2026-11-03.txt),
one `owner/repo` per line. One command audits all of it and leaves the repairs
in `/tmp/repairs`:

```sh
$ dsh-plugin audit --remote --from docs/ecosystem-audit-2026-11-0
